blog_personal_03_glm.text:
Grading papers beats billable hours: my first semester as a teacher

Last August, I left Hendricks & Cole after fourteen years as a corporate attorney and walked into Room 214 at Roosevelt High School with a provisional teaching license and a healthy dose of terror. I turned 42 in October, and it was the first birthday in a decade I didn't spend answering emails from my phone.

People ask why I left. In 2022 I defended a merger that eliminated 300 jobs in a town of 8,000 people, and I couldn't stop thinking about it. My sister, who has taught fourth grade in Duluth for twenty years, told me something that stuck: "You keep calculating what things cost. Try calculating what things are worth."

This semester I've been teaching eleventh-grade civics and one section of constitutional law (yes, our district actually offers it).

I make $52,400 a year. In 2019, I made that by March. But I've never once eaten dinner at my desk, and I quit my migraine medication in November because (knock on wood) I stopped needing it.

The learning curve humbled me. I spent twelve years at Yale Law and Big Law, and I genuinely believed classroom management would just be "leadership skills." It wasn't. It took me until late September to figure out that my third-period class, thirty-one sophomores, would settle down only if I let Marcus open class with his "news of the day" recap. It's now the best part of my mornings.

The hardest week was October 16th, when I stayed late for parent-teacher conferences and six parents asked, some suspiciously, why a lawyer would want *their kids*. I told them the truth: a girl in my second-period civics class named Priya had asked whether the First Amendment protects her TikTok, and it was the best question anyone had asked me in years.

Final exams ended December 20th. When I closed the gradebook, 84% of my students had passed, and one kid, Diego, told me he wants to be a lawyer now. I didn't cry, but it was close.

I still keep my bar card in my wallet. Some habits die hard. But when the bell rings at 7:45 tomorrow morning, I know exactly where I'd rather be.

blog_personal_13_luna.text:
In January 2025, my A1C was 8.4%, and I was tired of pretending that "eating pretty well" was a measurable plan. My doctor, Dr. Lena Morales at Kaiser Permanente in Sacramento, said medication was an option, but because I had no urgent symptoms, we agreed to try six months of carefully tracked food, walking, sleep, and weight loss first.

I bought a cheap spiral notebook and started writing down everything: meals, times, portions, and how I felt afterward. My first breakfast journal entry read: "7:30 a.m.: bagel with cream cheese, banana, coffee." Two hours later, my glucose was 196 mg/dL. I didn't panic, but I did notice a pattern. Toast, rice, cereal, and large portions of potatoes pushed my numbers up quickly.

By February, I was making eggs with spinach, plain Greek yogurt with walnuts, or leftover chicken and vegetables. I still ate tacos on Fridays at El Rincon on Fruitridge Road, but I had two instead of four and skipped the sugary horchata. After dinner, my wife, Marisol, and I walked around our neighborhood for 20 minutes. Eventually, those walks became 35 minutes, five nights a week.

The hardest part was consistency. At my grandson Mateo's birthday in April, I ate a slice of chocolate cake. I wrote it down instead of calling the day ruined. My journal helped me see that one dessert was not the problem; giving up for three weeks afterward was.

At my June appointment, my A1C had fallen to 7.1%. By September, it was 6.5%, and I was down 24 pounds from January. My latest test, on January 10, 2026, showed 6.1%. I have managed this year without diabetes medication, but only with regular appointments and my doctor's approval. I still check my glucose, and I know my plan could change.

The notebooks are now stacked beside my coffee maker. They contain plenty of imperfect days, but also proof that small decisions (less rice, more vegetables, a walk after dinner) can add up to a completely different year.

blog_personal_05_sonnet.text:
Landed at Kansai on a Tuesday in October with ¥15,000 (about $100) a day as the ceiling, and left convinced Kyoto is one of the easier cities to do this in. You trade taxis for a bicycle and Michelin stars for tofu shops.

Day one. Haikyu Hostel near Kyoto Station, ¥3,400 a night for a dorm bed, ICOCA card loaded at the station kiosk. I rented a bike from the hostel for ¥800/day instead of taking buses, since Kyoto is flat and bike lanes are everywhere. Breakfast was a pastry and coffee from a Lawson konbini, ¥450. I rode to Fushimi Inari before 8am, ahead of the tour buses. The gates are free and you can walk up to the Yotsutsuji overlook in about 40 minutes. Lunch was kitsune soba at a standing counter near the shrine, ¥600. In the afternoon I went to Tofuku-ji (¥500 entry) for the garden, then biked to Gion and just walked. Wandering Hanamikoji Street costs nothing, and neither does Yasaka Shrine. Dinner was a bowl of ramen at a counter spot in Pontocho, ¥900, plus a can of Asahi from a vending machine, ¥150. Day total: about ¥10,200, under budget.

Day two. I skipped the hostel breakfast and grabbed onigiri from a konbini, ¥300. Then I biked out to Arashiyama for the bamboo grove, which is free and best before 9am, when it's just you and the creak of the stalks. Tenryu-ji temple next door is ¥500 and worth it for the pond garden. I crossed Togetsukyo Bridge, then had a cheap curry lunch near the station, ¥750. Early afternoon went to grazing at Nishiki Market instead of a sit-down meal: a skewer here, a piece of tamagoyaki there, maybe ¥1,200 total for enough food to count as lunch and a snack. I saw Kiyomizu-dera in late afternoon light, ¥400 entry, then walked down through Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka, which cost nothing and are the best-looking streets in the city. Last dinner was katsu curry, ¥1,100.

Two days and two nights cost roughly ¥19,000 total, so I banked almost a full extra day's budget by day two. What made it work was visiting temples before the crowds, which also means before you're tempted to buy overpriced tea to escape them, and letting a bike replace half your transit budget.

essay_opinion_16_luna.text:
At 8:47 p.m. last Tuesday, I ordered milk, bananas, and a bag of rice from QuickCart, the grocery app that promises delivery in fifteen minutes. At 8:59, a rider in a blue helmet left the order outside my apartment on Valencia Street. It felt miraculous until I saw him sprint back to his electric bike, already checking the next notification.

The fifteen-minute promise has changed the streets in my neighborhood. QuickCart and DashBasket opened dark grocery warehouses nearby in 2024, and since then delivery riders idle beside every corner store, their bikes blocking curb cuts and bus stops. They work in rain, heat, and the late-night quiet. They are paid per delivery, and several riders I've spoken with said they are penalized when an order arrives late. The speed I experience as convenience is pressure passed on to someone else.

Treating a carton of eggs like an emergency has a human cost. Riders weave through traffic on Valencia and 24th Street, racing the app's countdown clock. I have watched them mount the sidewalk to get around a double-parked van, or wait outside in December darkness because an apartment building has a locked lobby. One rider told me he made $118 over a ten-hour shift last Saturday, before expenses. That is less than a delivery scooter battery costs, and rent in San Francisco is far higher.

It has a neighborhood cost too. The small markets that once knew their customers now compete with companies backed by millions in venture capital and built for impulse purchases. The warehouses have no café, no bulletin board, no elderly neighbor asking about your family. They are anonymous rooms built to turn hunger, forgetfulness, and boredom into transactions.

I still use the service. Sometimes my disabled neighbor needs groceries, or I realize at 9 p.m. that I'm out of medicine and can't leave work. But I'm trying to be honest about what "instant" means. Food doesn't appear any faster. Another person absorbs the inconvenience, on a bike, in traffic, for a wage that barely covers the cost of staying in the city. Our groceries may arrive in fifteen minutes. The bill, as usual, comes later.

essay_opinion_04_luna.text:
The first thing Lisbon's housing crisis taught me about digital nomads is that "living anywhere" usually means living somewhere someone else can no longer afford.

I arrived in Lisbon in October 2022 with a suitcase and the usual story: I worked online, got paid in dollars, and wanted to experience the city slowly. My apartment in Arroios cost €1,150 a month, more than many local salaries, and it counted as a bargain because the lease was only three months. The landlord had previously rented it to tourists through Airbnb.

At the cafés around Intendente and Graça, I met other remote workers comparing neighborhoods, Wi-Fi speeds, and visa options. We talked enthusiastically about "community" and rarely about the people who had been pushed out of it. A bartender told me she and her partner had moved to Setúbal after their rent went up by €300. Her commute to central Lisbon took nearly two hours each way. She hadn't been looking for a lifestyle. She needed a home.

Digital nomadism turns geography into an arbitrage opportunity. We bring salaries earned in richer economies into places where housing markets are already under pressure. Individually, we may be polite and curious and careful with our recycling. Together, we can still make a neighborhood less livable for the people who built it.

Foreigners are not uniquely to blame for Lisbon's housing crisis. Years of speculation, short-term rentals, weak tenant protections, and stagnant wages matter more than any single group of newcomers. But nomads are part of the demand, and our language hides that. We call ourselves flexible when what we really have is purchasing power.

Now, when I hear someone praise the freedom of working from anywhere, I think of that bartender's commute. "Anywhere" has schools, grandparents, rent-controlled apartments, and residents whose lives don't come with a return flight.

I'd like nomads to ask "Can I afford to live here?" and also "What happens to this place if thousands of people like me decide that we can?

essay_opinion_12_glm.text:
We started the four-day trial last October, mostly because our operations manager, Priya, wouldn't stop forwarding us articles about it. There are twenty-two of us at a logistics software company in Leeds, and we'd been losing people, with three resignations that summer alone. So on a gray Tuesday, the directors announced we'd close the office every Friday for six months and see what happened.

I expected chaos. Instead the performative meeting mostly died off.

Getting used to the fifth day off was easy. What took longer was noticing how much of our four days had been theater. The Monday status meeting that ran ninety minutes got cut to twenty-five, because suddenly everyone had somewhere to be: their lives. The "quick syncs" that were really people avoiding written decisions disappeared. By November our team chat had an unspoken rule: if it can be a message, it's a message.

The numbers improved too. Customer ticket response time dropped 14%. Nobody worked harder. Tom finally had time to rebuild the ticket-routing system he'd been "meaning to get to" for two years. We didn't actually use Fridays for that kind of work. Just knowing Friday was coming gave us guilt-free space during the week.

The bigger change was cultural, and it happened slowly. People started admitting when they were stuck. I think the four-day week made an implicit promise that your time is valuable, so we won't waste it, and once that promise was on the table, wasting your own time felt sillier. Our junior developer, Marcus, asked for help on a problem in week two that he told me later he'd normally have hidden for a month.

Not everything worked. Two clients initially hated losing Friday contact until we moved their support rotations. One colleague, Dillon, kept working Fridays from home out of habit, and it took a direct conversation to convince him the point wasn't to squeeze five days into four.

When the trial ended in April, the vote to keep it was 21-1. Dillon voted yes.

I've stopped thinking of it as a scheduling change. With less time to fill, we had fewer excuses, and most of what we called collaboration turned out to be mutual avoidance with a calendar invite attached.

essay_opinion_00_glm.text:
I joined Instagram in October 2013, back when you could only post square photos and my biggest concern was choosing a filter. Clarendon, mostly. Last month, on a Tuesday evening in March, I deleted the app after eleven years and roughly 14,000 posts, stories, and likes.

It wasn't a dramatic decision. There was no scandal, data breach, or public manifesto. What finally did it was embarrassingly small: I caught myself watching a reel of a stranger renovating a camper van in Portugal while my six-year-old narrated a drawing she'd made me, and I said "uh-huh" four times without hearing a word. She stopped mid-sentence. That pause was worse than any screen-time report.

I'd tried moderation before. Gray-scale mode, app timers, the whole digital-minimalism cottage industry. The minutes were part of it, since two-plus hours a day, according to my iPhone's screen-time settings, wasn't nothing. But mostly Instagram had become the shape of my attention itself. I experienced meals, sunsets, my own garden as pre-content. I once rearranged a plate of pasta at my aunt's house in Yonkers for better light. She still brings it up.

What surprised me most was what the habit was actually made of. It was idle hands and threshold moments: waking up, waiting for coffee, standing in line at the bodega. So I replaced the slots. Kindle in my pocket instead of my phone (I've finished nine books since March, up from three all of last year). A paper notebook for the bathroom-line impulse to check something, anything. Walking, badly and slowly, toward the subway instead of scrolling on the platform.

I won't pretend everything transformed. There were three ugly days of phantom-thumb swiping at a home screen where the app used to live. I still don't know what half my acquaintances are up to, and occasionally that stings. I missed a friend's engagement announcement and had to apologize with actual words.

What I didn't expect was that boredom came back. Real, fertile boredom, the kind that makes you notice you've been meaning to fix the wobbly chair for two years. I fixed it. Then I sat in the quiet and didn't photograph it for anyone.

If you're thinking about it, you don't need a better reason than wanting your own attention back. I waited eleven years for a good enough excuse. Turns out "I just wanted to" was enough.

essay_opinion_06_glm.text:
The first thing I did after landing at Haneda at 1 a.m. on a Tuesday in March was walk into a 7-Eleven and buy an onigiri. It was salmon, 140 yen, in plastic engineered to keep the seaweed crisp until you open it. I later learned the design was patented in the 1970s and has been refined for decades since. I ate it standing on the sidewalk in Meguro, jet-lagged and slightly delirious, and thought it was the best rice ball I'd ever had.

I've thought about that onigiri a lot since, because of what it says about Tokyo's convenience stores, the konbini. Japan has over 56,000 of them, more than 7,000 in Tokyo alone, so you're rarely more than a few hundred meters from one. We tend to treat them as a punchline about modern alienation, the lonely beacon of processed food glowing all night. After three years living in Nakano, I see them as some of the most sophisticated urban infrastructure anywhere.

Consider the logistics. A typical store restocks three times a day, and the bento is made that morning and discounted that evening. The system knows that a shōgayaki pork lunch sells in Shinjuku but not in Setagaya, and adjusts orders store by store. Nothing sits. The food is good, too. The karaage and egg sandwiches are reliable, and in winter there's oden simmering by the register. I've had worse meals at three times the price in New York.

The food is only part of it. You can pay your utility bills, print documents, buy concert tickets, ship luggage, and withdraw cash. The ATMs take foreign cards, which saved me more than once. When Tokyo's restaurants closed early during the pandemic, the konbini took on the city's eating hours without complaint. When the government launched its 2019 plastic bag fee, the stores adapted overnight.

What moves me most is the social role. The elderly man who comes in at 6:40 every morning for coffee and a copy of Sankei Shimbun is also checking in, and the clerk knows him. In a city of 37 million people, the konbini works like a corner store, run with terrifying precision but still somehow warm.

In the West we keep asking how to make cities more livable, more walkable, more human. Part of an answer might be on the corner of Koenji Dori at 3 a.m., fully lit, selling hot coffee, fried chicken, and umbrellas, and asking nothing of you except 130 yen.

essay_student_08_sonnet.text:
In June 2013, Edward Snowden, a 29-year-old contractor for Booz Allen Hamilton working at the National Security Agency's facility in Hawaii, gave journalists Glenn Greenwald and Laura Poitras thousands of classified documents. They detailed programs like PRISM and the bulk collection of American phone records under Section 215 of the Patriot Act. The Guardian first published his disclosures on June 6, 2013, and they set off a global debate over surveillance, privacy, and state secrecy. They also raised a harder question: when, if ever, is it right to break a sworn oath and the law to expose wrongdoing?

The case for Snowden rests on consequence and conscience. He revealed that the NSA was collecting metadata on millions of Americans with no individualized suspicion. Later that year, a federal judge, Richard Leon, called the program "almost Orwellian." Internal channels often fail, which is why whistleblowing of this kind matters. Snowden has said he raised concerns with colleagues and believed formal complaints would be buried or used against him. Utilitarian ethics can defend his choice: the public benefit of accountability, debate, and eventual reform outweighed the harm of exposure. That reform included the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015, which ended the bulk phone-records program.

The case against him is serious, though. Snowden violated the Espionage Act of 1917, broke an oath to protect classified information, and fled first to Hong Kong and then to Moscow, where he has lived since 2013. That raises the question of whether he acted on principle or to protect himself. Deontologists hold that rules and promises carry independent moral weight. An intelligence officer who unilaterally decides which secrets the public deserves to know sets a precedent that could endanger lives or paralyze legitimate security operations. Critics, including former NSA Director Michael Hayden, argued that Snowden had legal alternatives, such as the Intelligence Community Whistleblower Protection Act, even if those channels were imperfect.

The dilemma resists a clean resolution because two real goods conflict. One is the rule of law and institutional trust. The other is the public's right to know when a government oversteps its own boundaries in secret. Snowden's case suggests that whistleblowing is justified only under narrow conditions: the wrongdoing is systemic, the harm significant, and internal remedies genuinely exhausted. By that standard, his choice looks like a calculated gamble that the truth was worth the cost he knew he would pay, a description that fits neither treason nor heroism well.

forum_answer_10_luna.text:
For a 2-inch hole, use a self-adhesive metal drywall patch instead of filling the opening with joint compound alone.

First, trim away loose paper and square up any ragged edges with a utility knife. Wipe off dust. Center a metal mesh patch of 4 inches or larger over the hole and press it firmly so it lies flat. If the damage is near a corner or stud, make sure the patch does not bridge an uneven surface.

Cover the patch with setting-type joint compound, such as 45-minute Easy Sand. Use a 6-inch taping knife and feather the compound at least 3 inches beyond the patch. Let it harden, then scrape off ridges and apply a second, thinner coat. You may need a third skim coat to hide the patch completely.

After the final coat dries, usually overnight, sand lightly with 150- or 220-grit sandpaper. Run your hand over the area. If you can feel an edge, apply more compound instead of sanding aggressively. Wipe away dust, prime the repair with drywall primer, and paint with the matching wall color.

Since a door knob caused the hole, install a doorstop or hinge pin stop after repairing it. For a knob that hits the wall, a wall-mounted rubber stop is usually best. If the hole is close to an electrical outlet or switch, turn off the circuit before cutting or sanding, and don't drive screws in that area.

essay_student_12_glm.text:
Napoleon's 1812 invasion of Russia ended in disaster because of choices, above all his own. The invasion grew out of a political quarrel that never justified war on such a scale. Russia's Tsar Alexander I abandoned the Continental System, Napoleon's blockade of Britain, because it was strangling Russian trade in goods like timber and tallow. Napoleon did not negotiate or accept a compromise. He assembled the Grande Armée of roughly 600,000 men, the largest force Europe had ever seen, and crossed the Neman River on June 24, 1812.

The disaster could have been prevented at every stage. First, the timing was reckless. Napoleon invaded late in June, gambling that he could force a decisive battle and compel Alexander to sue for peace within a few weeks. The Russians under Barclay de Tolly and then Mikhail Kutuzov refused to be pinned down. They withdrew eastward and burned supplies as they went, and the campaign became a chase without a victory. Napoleon won the costly Battle of Borodino on September 7, with some 70,000 total casualties, and reached Moscow that month. He found the city ablaze and Alexander refusing to negotiate. An emperor of Napoleon's intelligence should have had contingency plans for exactly this scenario. Instead he lingered in Moscow for over a month, waiting for a letter that never came, until the onset of winter forced a retreat.

Second, the logistics were knowingly inadequate. Napoleon planned to feed his army partly through magazines and partly by foraging, but the Russian scorched-earth strategy and the vast distances made this impossible. Horses died by the tens of thousands, and typhus and dysentery ravaged the ranks before a single major battle was fought. Historians estimate that of the 600,000 who entered Russia, fewer than 100,000 returned. A less ambitious force with secure supply lines, or a limited campaign aimed at Lithuania and Belorussia, might have achieved a negotiated settlement without catastrophe.

Defenders of Napoleon argue that his position as hegemon of Europe required enforcing the Continental System, and that allowing Russia's defiance would have encouraged Austria and Prussia to defect. This has some weight, but it explains the invasion's motive, not its execution. Diplomatic pressure, a show of force in Poland, or even a smaller punitive campaign were available alternatives.

The invasion was preventable. It came from overconfidence and poor intelligence, and from Napoleon's inability to imagine that an opponent would simply refuse to play his game. His own assumptions defeated him more than Russian arms did.

forum_answer_00_glm.text:
A nail polish remover smell is normal for a young starter. It means fermentation is happening.

After about 48 to 72 hours, the wild yeast and bacteria in your flour start producing acetic acid and esters as they consume the starches. When the starter runs low on fresh food between feedings, the bacterial activity shifts and produces acetone-like compounds. This is especially common with whole grain flours (rye, whole wheat), which ferment faster and more aggressively than all-purpose.

To fix it:

1. Feed more frequently. For the next 3 to 4 days, feed your starter every 12 hours instead of every 24. Use a 1:1:1 ratio by weight (e.g., 50g starter, 50g flour, 50g water at roughly 78°F).

2. Check your flour-to-water balance. If your starter is too thin, acids build up faster. A slightly thicker consistency (equal parts by weight) slows that down.

3. Keep the temperature steady. If your counter is above 75°F (near an oven or in a warm kitchen), fermentation speeds up and the starter burns through its food quickly. Aim for 68 to 75°F. I keep mine next to the coffee maker, away from the stove, and it made a huge difference.

Around days 4 to 6 the smell often gets *worse* before it gets better. It can shift to gym socks or vomit-like odors as different bacterial populations compete. Don't dump it. By days 7 to 10, most starters settle into a pleasant yeasty, slightly tangy, apple-cider-vinegar smell and rise reliably, doubling within 4 to 6 hours of feeding.

Worry only if you see pink or orange streaks (mold) or fuzzy growth on the surface. The acetone smell alone is no reason to discard the starter. It's just hungry, and a consistent feeding schedule will normalize it.

I've kept the same starter going since March 2021, and it smelled like a nail salon every time I neglected it a day too long.

forum_answer_16_luna.text:
For a table named `users` with an `email` column, group by the email address and keep groups with more than one row:

```sql
SELECT
    email,
    COUNT(*) AS duplicate_count
FROM users
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY duplicate_count DESC, email;
```

This returns each duplicated address and the number of times it appears. For example, if `alex@example.com` appears 3 times, the result includes:

```text
alex@example.com | 3
```

If addresses that differ only in capitalization or surrounding spaces should count as duplicates, normalize them in the query:

```sql
SELECT
    LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalized_email,
    COUNT(*) AS duplicate_count
FROM users
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY duplicate_count DESC;
```

To retrieve the user records involved, join against that query as a derived table:

```sql
SELECT u.*
FROM users AS u
JOIN (
    SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalized_email
    FROM users
    WHERE email IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
) AS d
  ON LOWER(TRIM(u.email)) = d.normalized_email
ORDER BY d.normalized_email, u.id;
```

With 2 million rows this is still an ordinary aggregation query, but an index on the normalized value can speed it up if your database supports one. For PostgreSQL:

```sql
CREATE INDEX users_email_normalized_idx
ON users (LOWER(TRIM(email)));
```

If duplicates are not allowed, enforce uniqueness for future inserts. In PostgreSQL, for example:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_unique_idx
ON users (LOWER(TRIM(email)))
WHERE email IS NOT NULL;
```

Clean up the existing duplicates, or decide how to handle them, before adding that constraint. The index creation fails while duplicate normalized addresses remain.

memo_policy_05_sonnet.text:
TO: Executive Steering Committee
FROM: Finance & IT Strategy
RE: ERP cloud migration, cost-benefit summary
DATE: September 21, 2026

## Recommendation

Approve the $2.3M migration of our on-premises SAP ECC 6.0 environment to a cloud-based SaaS ERP (S/4HANA Cloud), with go-live targeted for Q3 2027.

## Cost basis

The $2.3M upfront investment covers data migration and cleansing ($620K), integration rebuilds for 14 connected systems including our WMS and Salesforce instance ($540K), retraining for 180 finance and operations users ($310K), dual-running costs during a four-month parallel cutover ($450K), and contingency and PM overhead ($380K).

The annual SaaS subscription is $890K. Current on-prem maintenance, hosting, and support cost $1.15M a year, so the run-rate savings are $260K annually.

## Payback

Three things feed the payback calculation: the $260K in run-rate savings, a planned $1.4M server refresh we would no longer need (deferred capex avoided in FY2027), and estimated productivity gains of $310K a year from automated workflows. Together they bring payback in 3.1 years and a 5-year NPV of about $1.7M at our 8% discount rate.

## Compliance

Our SOC 2 Type II and GDPR obligations (the latter because of our EU subsidiary in Dublin) require contractual data residency guarantees from the vendor. Legal has confirmed that the proposed vendor's EU data center meets this requirement.

SOX change-management controls will need updated documentation for the new release cadence, since the SaaS vendor pushes quarterly updates that we do not control.

## Risks

The two main risks are disruption to month-end close during cutover and resistance to change among tenured finance staff. The parallel-run period mitigates the first, and the retraining budget above addresses the second.

## Next step

We need committee approval by October 10, 2026 to lock vendor pricing before their November rate increase.

paper_section_01_luna.text:
AlphaFold2, announced after the 2020 CASP14 assessment and published in *Nature* in 2021, changed protein structure prediction. Its Evoformer repeatedly exchanged information between multiple-sequence-alignment (MSA) and residue-pair representations through attention and outer-product updates. A structure module based on invariant point attention (IPA) then converted these representations into three-dimensional coordinates. The model combined sequence evolution with geometric reasoning and recycled its intermediate predictions, and it achieved a median GDT-TS score of 92.4 in CASP14, with a median of 87.0 on difficult free-modeling targets. IPA's attention operates on learned three-dimensional points while remaining invariant to global rotations and translations. ([Jumper et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2))

Later architectures built on this attention-centered design in different ways. RoseTTAFold, developed at the University of Washington and reported in *Science* in 2021, used a three-track network that simultaneously processed one-dimensional sequence/MSA features, two-dimensional residue-pair information, and three-dimensional coordinates. Attention, graph-transformer operations, and SE(3)-equivariant layers let information circulate among these representations. For proteins shorter than 400 residues, its end-to-end implementation generated backbone coordinates in approximately 10 minutes on an RTX 2080 GPU. ([Baek et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj8754)) In parallel, protein language models treated structure prediction as a consequence of learning representations at the scale of sequences. Meta's ESM-2 and ESMFold used Transformer language-model embeddings to predict structures from single sequences, which avoids the computational cost of explicit MSAs. ESMFold, published in *Science* in 2023, enabled the ESM Metagenomic Atlas, which contains predictions for more than 617 million proteins, although its accuracy generally remained below AlphaFold2's. ([Lin et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ade2574))

AlphaFold3, published in *Nature* in 2024, moved from protein folding toward modeling biomolecular interactions. It replaced AlphaFold2's IPA-based structure module with a diffusion-based generative architecture that can jointly model proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, ions, and modified residues. Transformer-based protein prediction has thus gone from MSA-conditioned geometric attention to multimodal foundation models that combine language representations, equivariant geometry, and diffusion-based coordinate generation.

MEMORANDUM

To: All Department Heads and Regional Managers
From: Priya Nair, Director of Human Resources
Date: April 14, 2025
Re: Remote work eligibility revisions and results of the March staff survey

Purpose

This memo summarizes findings from the March 2025 remote work survey (1,240 respondents, an 82% response rate) and announces revised eligibility criteria effective June 2, 2025.

Survey findings

- 74% of respondents support a hybrid model; only 11% prefer full-time office attendance.
- Productivity self-ratings were equal or higher for remote days in 87% of responses.
- Departments with fixed in-office mandates (Facilities, Front Desk Services, Print Production) reported the lowest satisfaction scores.
- 63% of staff cited commuting costs as a significant concern, averaging $340/month.

Revised policy, effective June 2, 2025

1. Standard hybrid schedule: Eligible employees may work remotely up to three days per week, increased from two, with manager approval.
2. Fully remote classification: Roles designated as location-independent (currently 112 positions across IT, Finance, and Marketing) may be performed fully remotely, subject to quarterly performance reviews.
3. In-office essential roles: Positions requiring physical presence (building security, mailroom, and lab technicians at the Portland and Denver sites) remain onsite, with a commuting stipend of $75/month.
4. Eligibility threshold: Employees must have completed six months of service (previously twelve) and maintain a performance rating of "Meets Expectations" or higher.

Implementation requirements

- Managers must submit updated team hybrid agreements to HR by May 16, 2025.
- All staff must complete the revised Remote Work Agreement in Workday by May 30, 2025.
- Remote employees within 50 miles of the Denver, Austin, or Boston offices must attend onsite once per month for team collaboration days.

Compliance notes

Remote arrangements remain contingent on state tax and labor law compliance in the employee's work location. Requests to relocate out of state require 60 days' advance notice and HR Legal review.

Send questions to hr-policy@company.com or raise them at the April 24 all-hands briefing.

paper_section_07_luna.text:
We conducted a field experiment from October 2023 to August 2024 among 1,150 smallholder farmers cultivating vegetables in Kenya's Makueni and Kitui counties. Households were identified through village-level agricultural registers and screened for eligibility: respondents had to cultivate between 0.1 and 2.0 hectares, rely primarily on rain-fed or manually irrigated production, and not currently use drip irrigation. After baseline surveys, farmers were stratified by county and baseline irrigated area and randomly assigned to one of three groups: information only (n = 383), information plus a 50% voucher for a drip-irrigation kit (n = 384), or information plus a 75% voucher (n = 383).

All treatment households attended a two-hour demonstration conducted by locally trained agricultural extension agents in November 2023. The sessions explained installation, maintenance, expected water savings, and crop-specific application rates using a 0.1-hectare demonstration plot. Vouchers were redeemable through participating agro-dealers in Makueni and Kitui until February 29, 2024. Each kit included a 500-liter storage tank, a low-pressure filter, 100 meters of lateral tubing, and connectors, and was estimated to irrigate 0.1 hectare. Farmers in the information-only group received the same technical information but no price subsidy.

Enumerators who were blinded to treatment assignment conducted in-person surveys at baseline, four months after voucher expiration, and at the end of the 2024 main growing season. The primary outcome was adoption, defined as installation and use of a drip system on at least 0.05 hectares during the 30 days preceding the endline survey. Secondary outcomes included cultivated area, irrigation frequency, input expenditures, vegetable yields, farm revenue, water use, and reported labor requirements. Crop production was measured using farmer records and randomly selected crop-cutting plots. We estimated intention-to-treat effects using ordinary least squares, controlling for county fixed effects and pre-specified baseline covariates, with standard errors clustered at the village level.

paper_section_21_glm.text:
# Introduction

Chemotherapy dosing is one of the most consequential and least optimized decisions in oncology care. Standard-of-care regimens for cytotoxic agents such as 5-fluorouracil, carboplatin, and doxorubicin were largely established through population-level dose-finding trials in the 1980s and 1990s. Doses were typically fixed at body-surface-area-normalized amounts, with protocol-mandated reductions for toxicity. This one-size-fits-all approach ignores the large inter- and intra-patient pharmacokinetic variability of cytotoxic therapy, where drug clearance often differs more than 10-fold. The clinical consequences are well documented. Undertreatment compromises tumor control, while overtreatment produces grade 3 or 4 neutropenia, neuropathy, and treatment discontinuation. In metastatic colorectal cancer, for example, retrospective analyses of FOLFOX administration found that fewer than 30% of patients received what post hoc modeling suggests was the optimally tolerated dose trajectory.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is a natural framework for this sequential decision-making problem. Dosing can be formulated as a Markov decision process. At each treatment cycle, the clinician observes a state (blood counts, toxicity grades, biomarkers, performance status), selects an action (dose level, timing, or agent modification), and receives a reward that reflects the trade-off between tumor response and cumulative toxicity. Early proof-of-concept work by Zhao et al. (2011) showed that a fully observable RL agent trained on simulated patient data could outperform fixed protocols in a compartmental model of myelosuppression. More recently, offline RL methods, including conservative Q-learning, behavior-cloned policy constraints, and doubly robust off-policy evaluation, have made it possible to learn from observational electronic health record data without risky online exploration in vulnerable populations. The TempoRL initiative (2022 to 2024) and related dose-optimization efforts at institutions including MD Anderson and Duke have begun moving these methods toward prospective evaluation.

Significant barriers still separate retrospective RL benchmarks from deployable trial interventions. These include partial observability of disease burden, non-stationarity of patient physiology over treatment courses, conservative safety constraints, and regulatory uncertainty under FDA guidance on adaptive trial designs and AI/ML-based software as a medical device. In this paper, we review how adaptive chemotherapy dosing is formulated as an RL problem and evaluate the methodological strengths and limitations of published approaches. We also propose a trial design, incorporating off-policy confidence bounds and a clinician-in-the-loop policy veto, which we argue is a necessary precondition for first-in-human evaluation.

Day 90. Down 22 lbs (194→172), squat 1RM up from 135 to 225, and I can finally do a dead hang pull-up (couldn't do one on Day 1). I ran the numbers this morning before writing this up, so figured I'd share the whole thing.

The program was a modified PPL split, 5 days/week, at a globo gym near my apartment in Raleigh. I started June 23rd and finished September 20th. I tracked everything in a notes app: every set, and every meal (roughly, MyFitnessPal for calories, no macro obsessing).

Numbers:
- Weight: 194 → 172 lbs
- Waist: 38" → 33"
- Squat: 135x5 → 225x5
- Bench: 115x5 → 175x5
- Deadlift: 185x5 → 275x5
- Mile time: 11:40 → 8:55 (didn't train for this, just noticed it dropping)

What worked: I ate at a ~500 cal deficit for the first 60 days, then a slight surplus for the last 30 to try to push strength. I probably should've just stayed in deficit longer, since weight results plateaued around week 10. Sleep tracking mattered more than I expected. Anything under 6.5 hours and my lifts the next day were noticeably worse.

What I'd do differently: I skipped almost all mobility and stretching work, and my hips are paying for it now. I also under-ate protein for the first 3 weeks (averaging like 90g/day at 194 lbs, way too low) before I started actually weighing food.

If you've done a similar cut-then-lean-bulk cycle, how long did you wait before starting the next block? I'm thinking of taking 2 weeks totally off before round two.

paper_section_03_glm.text:
## Results

Adding cesium bromide (CsBr) to the methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI₃) perovskite precursor solution significantly improved power conversion efficiency (PCE). Champion devices made with 5 mol% CsBr reached a PCE of 19.4%, against 18.1% for undoped controls. That is a 7.2% relative improvement, or 1.3 percentage points absolute. The result was reproduced across three independent fabrication batches prepared between March and May 2024, with champion-device PCEs of 19.1 to 19.6% for CsBr-doped cells and 17.8 to 18.3% for controls.

Current density-voltage (J-V) measurements under AM 1.5G illumination (100 mW cm⁻²) showed that the gain came mainly from a higher open-circuit voltage (V_OC): 1.12 ± 0.02 V for doped devices versus 1.06 ± 0.03 V for controls (n = 24 devices per condition, p < 0.001, two-tailed t-test). Short-circuit current density (J_SC) rose modestly from 22.4 ± 0.6 to 22.9 ± 0.5 mA cm⁻², while fill factor did not change significantly (FF = 0.74 ± 0.02 in both groups). Hysteresis indices fell from 8.3% to 4.1% with CsBr, consistent with reduced ion migration.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) of the doped films showed the (110) reflection shifted 0.14° toward higher 2θ and the PbI₂ peak at 12.7° suppressed. This indicates partial substitution of Cs⁺ into the A-site and improved phase purity. Scanning electron microscopy showed larger grains (mean grain size 412 ± 95 nm versus 287 ± 78 nm for controls), which correlated with lower trap-state density, from 1.8 × 10¹⁶ to 1.1 × 10¹⁶ cm⁻³, measured by space-charge-limited current analysis.

Under continuous illumination at 65 °C, doped devices kept 88% of their initial PCE after 500 hours, versus 74% for controls. Doping above 5 mol% (tested at 10 and 15 mol%) caused phase segregation and lower performance (PCE 17.2% and 15.9%, respectively), so 5 mol% CsBr was the optimum within the compositions studied.

Grant Progress Report: NSF Award #2145987
Reporting period: Year 2, Q3 (July 1 to September 21, 2026)
PI: Dr. Rachel Ostrander, Department of Materials Science, Purdue University

Summary: Year 2 of the award ("Scalable Synthesis of Anisotropic Nanocomposites for Low-Energy Thermal Regulation") had five milestones. Three are complete.

Milestone 1, reactor scale-up (completed May 2026): The 5-liter continuous-flow reactor was commissioned in the West Lafayette lab. Yield consistency across 40 batch runs was 92%, above the 85% target.

Milestone 2, anisotropic alignment protocol (completed July 2026): Graduate student Wei Chen developed a magnetic-field-assisted alignment method that reached an order parameter of 0.87. The work was published in the August 2026 issue of Advanced Materials Interfaces.

Milestone 3, thermal conductivity benchmarking (completed September 15, 2026): Postdoc Dr. Amara Osei benchmarked the material against 12 commercial composites at Argonne National Laboratory's CNM facility. Cross-plane thermal conductivity was 34% lower than the isotropic baseline.

Remaining milestones: Milestone 4 (durability testing under 500 thermal cycles) is 60% complete, and full data are expected by December 2026. Milestone 5 (integration into a prototype thermal barrier device) has not started. Our fabrication partner, Sandia National Laboratories, has confirmed device housing availability for January 2027.

Budget: We have spent $412,000 of the $580,000 Year 2 allocation (71%), which is on track with the approved spend plan.

Personnel: Undergraduate researcher Marcus Devine joined the team in June 2026, supported through the REU supplement.

Next reporting period: We will finish the Milestone 4 cycling data and begin Milestone 5 device integration before the Year 2 annual report is due on March 1, 2027.

I just hired 12 junior developers at Shopify, and I went through 400+ resumes to do it. Here is what got my attention.

1. Projects that solved real problems. I don't need your Netflix clone. One candidate built a scheduling tool for her mom's dental clinic in Mississauga. It had auth, a real database, and actual users. That beat every todo app in the stack.

2. Evidence that you can learn fast. A 3-month bootcamp certificate matters less than a GitHub history with steady commits over 12+ months, even on tiny projects. I'd take consistency over intensity.

3. Writing that respects my time. Short resumes won. The best bullet points said what you built, with what, and what happened ("cut page load from 4s to 1.2s"). One page was plenty. You're juniors, and we expect that.

4. Signs of curiosity. Blog posts, Stack Overflow answers, a question in a PR description. Two hires came straight from strong code review comments on open-source repos.

5. What didn't matter: brand-name schools (5 of 12 were self-taught), cover letter length (one paragraph was fine), and knowing our exact stack. We teach Rails internally in week one.

The biggest surprise was that only 9 of 400 resumes mentioned accessibility or testing. If you're a junior looking for an edge in 2024, start there.

To the 12 who joined us in January: welcome to the team. To everyone else: keep building, keep shipping.

We're opening the next cohort this fall. 👀

report_work_15_glm.text:
Field research log: bird population counts, Cedar Swamp
Week of May 6 to 15, 2024
Submitted by: Dana Whitfield, Field Technician, Northline Audubon Society

## Summary of activity

Over ten consecutive survey days, our three-person team (D. Whitfield, M. Okafor, and intern J. Reyes) completed 40 point-count surveys across the Cedar Swamp monitoring grid. We covered all eight established stations in both the morning (0530 to 0900) and evening (1700 to 1930) windows. Weather was generally cooperative. Only the May 9 morning count was cut short, by heavy rain.

## Results

We recorded 42 species, up from 37 during the same period last year, and 1,184 individual detections. Notable observations:

- Virginia rail: detected at Station 3 on four occasions, suggesting a possible breeding pair. It was last confirmed in 2019.
- Prothonotary warbler: a single male sang at Station 6 on May 11 and May 13. Flagged for follow-up nest-box evaluation.
- Great blue heron: an active rookery near the north dike with at least 6 occupied nests.
- Swamp sparrow and common yellowthroat: the most abundant species, together roughly 22% of all detections.

Abundance by station was uneven. Stations 3 and 6 accounted for 38% of total detections, likely reflecting the expanded emergent marsh habitat following last fall's hydrology restoration.

Data entry is complete in eBird and the internal Northline database. Audio recordings from the autonomous recording units (ARUs) at Stations 2 and 7 still need review. J. Reyes will process them by May 22.

## Issues and recommendations

1. The boardwalk between Stations 4 and 5 is deteriorating, and two planks are loose. I recommend maintenance before the June survey round.
2. Mosquito populations are high this season, so teams should carry repellent for the remaining spring counts.
3. Given the prothonotary warbler detection, I recommend deploying two nest boxes near Station 6 before June 1.

## Next steps

The second survey round runs June 3 to 12. Team assignments will be circulated by May 27. Please direct questions to me at d.whitfield@northlineaudubon.org.

1/3 I cold-emailed 200 VCs for my seed round in spring 2024 and made 5 mistakes.

Mistake #1: I sent the same generic pitch to everyone. "Hi, we're building the future of collaboration" meant nothing to a fintech investor in New York or a healthcare investor in Boston.

Mistake #2: I led with product features and buried our traction. Our strongest proof was $18,400 MRR and 37% month-over-month growth in March, and it sat on slide 12.

2/3 Mistake #3: I emailed partners who never invest at the seed stage. Several managed $500M+ funds but wrote their first checks at Series A. I should have read their websites and recent deals before reaching out.

Mistake #4: I asked for "15 minutes to connect." A clear, specific ask works better: "Would you consider leading a $1.5M seed round for a B2B workflow tool growing 37% MoM?"

3/3 Mistake #5: I followed up emotionally and inconsistently. Some VCs got four emails in 10 days, and others got none after the first message. My eventual system was simple: 3 follow-ups over 21 days, each with a new data point.

We closed the round in July 2024. The biggest lesson: sending 200 messages mattered less than relevance, proof, and timing.

1/ Last month my Etsy shop did $4,200 in revenue (August 1 to 31). After Etsy fees, shipping, materials, and ads, I kept about $2,180 as profit. Here's what sold:

2/ Best seller: personalized walnut recipe boards, 38 orders and $1,710 in revenue. Most buyers were ordering wedding gifts, and "Grandma's Kitchen" outsold every other customization.

3/ Second: birth flower art prints, 64 orders and $960 in revenue. They were inexpensive to make and had the best margin, especially the digital downloads. August's top combination was May + September flowers.

4/ Third: engraved dog tags, 29 orders and $725 in revenue. "Luna," "Charlie," and "Milo" were the most common names. My $3 personalization upgrade converted better than I expected.

5/ Everything else (stickers, keychains, and a new mug design) brought in $805 combined. The mugs got plenty of favorites but only 6 sales, so I'm pausing that line for now.

6/ Pinterest brought 41% of traffic, Etsy search brought 37%, and Instagram brought just 8%. My biggest day was August 12, after a Pinterest pin took off.

7/ Biggest lesson: the products with the strongest emotional angle (family, pets, milestones) sold best. For September I'm doubling down on personalized gifts and cutting anything people only "liked" but didn't buy.
